newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan's comments seen reining in stocks.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan's comments seen reining in stocks.

text.p: Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan on Wednesday questioned the sustainability of the U.S. stock market's sharp rise, and this time Wall Street may heed his warning.
The Dow industrials shot up 10 percent in the weeks after Greenspan first warned of "irrational exuberance" in financial markets on December 6.
But market analysts said the Fed chairman's latest comments add to a growing mood of caution on Wall Street and a repeat of that rally in the weeks ahead is unlikely.
"We all know Papa Greenspan is watching us," said Marshall Acuff, portfolio strategist at Smith Barney.
The Dow was down 80 points, or 1.1 percent, to 6957 in Wednesday afternoon trading.

In his semiannual economic report to Congress on Wednesday, Greenspan said caution was especially warranted with regard to the sharp rise in stock prices over the past two years. "These gains have obviously raised questions of sustainability," he said.
Market analysts said they did not think the comments in themselves would lead to a major downturn in stocks. But they said they could serve to constrain any near-term rally.

Technical analysts and some Wall Street bulls, including Abby Cohen of Goldman Sachs, have said they expect U.S. stocks to move in a sideways, trading-range pattern over the near term as the sharp gains of the start of the year are digested.

"The market is not drastically overvalued...but everybody is definitely edgy, I think motivated by wanting to preserve the fantastic gains of the last 27 months," said Charlie Crane, Spears Benzak Salomon and Farrell director of research.
Analysts said, however, it was far cry from a verbal warning from Greenspan to any action to constrain the market, such as a hike in near-term interest rates.
"It's a big gap between talk and doing something," Acuff said. "As long as (Greenspan) is not doing anything, then I don't think the market should sustain a big reaction."

Dan Ascani, president and director of research at Global Market Strategists Inc, said he had a more bearish view of Wall Street's near-term action. Greenspan's comments could speed up a move to bear market by convincing investors not to buy stocks on every dip in prices, he said.
"It may have changed the psychology at least," he said.
Crane said it would be key for Wall Street to see if Greenspan hedged his comments in the second day of his Humprhey-Hawkins report to Congress.
Greenspan's testimony to the House Banking sub-committee was postponed from Thursday to March 5 as Chilean President Eduardo Frei is due to address both houses of Congress tomorrow.
